props.title: Sleeping Beauty

sections.content: **Sleeping Beauty** (2011) marked a bold, unsettling debut from Julia Leigh, reimagining fairy tale elements through an erotic art-house lens. Like **Eyes Wide Shut** (1999) meets Belle de Jour (1967), it follows a college student who enters a mysterious high-end brothel where she's sedated and visited by elderly male clients. Emily Browning's fearless performance echoes the clinical detachment of **Under the Skin** (2013), while the film's stark compositions and long takes recall the formal control of Michael Haneke's **The Piano Teacher** (2001).

sections.content: The film sits within a wave of provocative female-directed explorations of sexuality and power from the 2010s. **The Girlfriend Experience** (2016) similarly examines transactional intimacy through a detached lens. **Raw** (2016) and **The Neon Demon** (2016) share Sleeping Beauty's interest in young women's bodies as sites of transformation and commodification. These films challenge conventional male-gaze narratives by maintaining uncomfortable distance rather than titillation. SUBHEAD: Clinical Eroticism and Body Politics

Leigh's clinical approach aligns with other contemporary directors interrogating sexuality through formal restraint. **Under the Skin** (2013) uses similar techniques of emotional removal, while **Elle** (2016) explores consent and power through equally complex means. The antiseptic chambers where Browning's character lies unconscious echo the sterile spaces of **Holy Motors** (2012) and **High Life** (2018), other films questioning bodily autonomy in modern society.
